</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:woven" data-paper-title="WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-multimodal-models-woven-63239e78" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7a31f3fc9074b0c6">Why isn&#x27;t WOVEN transition supervision ordinary static classification?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Awoven">WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northwestern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It models relations among initial state, action, and outcome, including forward prediction, inverse action, and counterfactuals. Generated video rollouts supply visual transitions and intermediate frames, not outcomes stated in prompts. Recognizing object classes is insufficient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same ball starts in one place but moves differently for left and right pushes; choose the action or outcome, not whether there is a ball.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12417">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.12417-woven/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7a31f3fc9074b0c6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:woven" data-paper-title="WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-507c29cd3a03e147">Why split WOVEN by initial scene or source rather than random QA rows?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Awoven">WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northwestern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One image can yield several actions, questions, and counterfactuals. Random row splits can put nearly identical states in both sets. Grouped isolation reduces shortcuts, and scene, action, and reasoning transfer need separate checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Group two questions about different pushes on the same table rather than splitting their common source across train and test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12417">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.12417-woven/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-507c29cd3a03e147">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:woven" data-paper-title="WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-9f43b6abf0908831">What distinct generalization problems do scene-OOD and state perturbation test?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Awoven">WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northwestern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Scene-OOD changes scene distribution; state perturbation changes state and tests robustness. High in-distribution accuracy does not solve either. The paper also controls action and reasoning axes, and per-benchmark subsets do not establish one universal model gain.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A new restaurant can be handled well while tiny object-position shifts in one scene still cause errors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12417">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.12417-woven/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9f43b6abf0908831">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:woven" data-paper-title="WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-def30335d1ff6136">What do four option permutations and source_id grouping guard against?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Awoven">WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Northwestern University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Move the correct letter with its option and image to prevent letter shortcuts. Split by initial source to prevent related variants leaking across sets. The prompt exposes only question, options, and actual images, not answer-related distractor_type. Local training runs SFT, not GRPO.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Put three questions from one initial frame together in train or holdout so source memorization cannot masquerade as test generalization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现, 代码映射与边界. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12417">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.12417-woven/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-def30335d1ff6136">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-gui-jepa-f231a89e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d61dbbeb9e00d39">Why doesn&#x27;t GUI-JEPA generate actions token by token?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It enumerates actions from the accessibility tree and conditions visual latents on each candidate, then scores the batch. The action space comes from observations rather than free-form text generation. Speed depends on candidate count and a11y input, which pixel-only agents may lack, so not all GUI systems are directly comparable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Score three valid button actions and choose the best, instead of generating JSON and parsing coordinates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d61dbbeb9e00d39">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-012814975154e4eb">Why route action and ROI through the residual predictor rather than directly to the structured scoring head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The paper forces candidate-conditioned visual information through the JEPA predictor rather than a shortcut. Action and ROI condition a query; a three-layer Transformer creates a residual latent, followed by ROI and global pooling. Training with a decision loss does not prove accurate future-screen prediction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Two click candidates with different ROI content and positions should give different latents. A bypass from raw ROI to the scorer cannot demonstrate predictor utility.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-012814975154e4eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e4c26d5506f18c85">How does GUI-JEPA scoring differ from predicting a next state and choosing the one closest to a goal?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Latents are decision features trained by listwise action loss; distance to a goal latent is not the value. A randomly initialized predictor can match a dynamics-pretrained one in the paper, so useful decision features are not necessarily good dynamics predictions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Confirming may finish a task with little visual change, while an animation looks closer to a target image but is wrong. Action score is not image or latent similarity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式, 论文离线与线上效果. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e4c26d5506f18c85">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:gui-jepa" data-paper-title="GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-3b5a93ef5e4fcae4">Does a verified three-layer predictor and gradient path mean the repository can operate Android?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Agui-jepa">GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-29 · Shanghai Jiao Tong University / Nanyang Technological University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It receives external screen/condition latents and verifies the residual head, candidate masking and weighted listwise loss. It has no encoder, a11y enumeration, MiniLM ranker or executor. Positive labels are loss-only, not forward inputs. A GPU tensor check is not AndroidControl success.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Backpropagating on two valid candidate latents only checks gradients. Launching an app also requires screen encoding, candidate discovery, execution and observing the next screen.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 检查与负控, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36877v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36877-gui-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3b5a93ef5e4fcae4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-foundation-models-swim-9da395d5" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-300d76e6b7918837">Does SWIM learn a robot policy or which state coordinates matter for distance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It learns continuous coordinate weights from recorded actions and uses them for world-model geometry. Inverse action prediction only trains the weights. Deployment still needs image encoding, latent dynamics and planning such as CEM. Local coverage is the gate objective and metric, not a robot policy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Block position can receive more weight than background light color. That changes distance, not the robot&#x27;s grasp trajectory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-300d76e6b7918837">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a40912dd5fb29c9d">Why not gate the current state, and why require true mismatched discrimination?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The current state is full action context; the paper gates only future displacement. Fitting positives alone can predict actions from current context and ignore displacement. A cyclic mismatch changes the future while holding current state/action fixed, encouraging behavior-relevant displacement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Keep the current position and move-right action. For a negative, take the next batch row&#x27;s future minus this position. Replacing the current state gives a spurious context cue.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a40912dd5fb29c9d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c1b394272419a8ac">Are multiplying state by g or sqrt(g), or standardizing again afterward, equivalent?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Square root scaling yields coefficient g in squared distance; scaling by g gives g². Gates weight already-standardized coordinates; re-standardization cancels scaling. Overall gate scale cancels from Pearson correlation and can be absorbed by the inverse model, so absolute gate magnitudes are not uniquely identifiable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: Difference 2 with g=0.25 should give 0.25×4=1. Multiplying by sqrt(g)=0.5 before squaring gives 1; multiplying by g gives 0.25. Rescaling the standard deviation afterward cancels the 0.5.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c1b394272419a8ac">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="foundation-models:swim" data-paper-title="SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="foundation-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0989a9f5d8371bbd">How do tests distinguish L1 shrinkage from learning behavior, and prevent future state leakage?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=foundation-models%3Aswim">SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-30 · Boston University / Unity Technologies</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Check gate gradients from the behavioral term alone, then real optimizer updates; parameter change alone is insufficient. In stage two state distance is stop-gradient. Future state constructs offline displacements only and must not be available to deployed planning. Constant-distance Pearson is undefined and should be rejected, not declared valid via arbitrary epsilon.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Example: λsum(g) shrinks gates even with actions ignored, so also test λ=0. If all frame distances are zero, reject the zero-denominator correlation rather than report success 1.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 检查与负控. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../foundation-models/2610.36662-swim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0989a9f5d8371bbd">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:rs-jepa" data-paper-title="RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<span id="paper-multimodal-models-rs-jepa-fcdebfcf" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-8a826054d2e3770a">How can changing only patch-reading order create different RS-JEPA self-supervised views?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Ars-jepa">RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-11 · Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Vision Mamba recurrence depends on preceding tokens, so identical pixels acquire different context under different paths. Position embeddings are added before sorting; encoding restores token order afterward. The change is scan dynamics, not pixels or hidden label augmentation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: a 2-by-3 grid has row order 0,1,2,3,4,5 and column order 0,3,1,4,2,5. The second patch already sees a different prefix.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14496">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../multimodal-models/2611.14496-rs-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8a826054d2e3770a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:rs-jepa" data-paper-title="RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-58ea66e7be7965f0">If forward tokens remain unchanged, how can the RS-JEPA scorer learn a harder partition?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Ars-jepa">RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-11 · Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Hard top-half membership selects views, while straight-through weights cancel to one in the forward pass but retain a sigmoid gradient path. Reversal updates the scorer toward harder prediction. Plain top-k slicing would sever that signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: unchanged forward tokens can yield a nonzero scorer gradient. Test exact outputs and reversed gradients, not just shapes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 核心公式, 数据协议与代码映射. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14496">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../multimodal-models/2611.14496-rs-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-58ea66e7be7965f0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:rs-jepa" data-paper-title="RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-eb1672b725d557bc">How does RS-JEPA neighbourhood consensus differ from aligning only registered twins?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Ars-jepa">RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-11 · Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Twin alignment brings the same scene together across sensors without ensuring agreement about other scenes. Consensus compares four neighbourhood distributions, excluding the paired index in every one. It supplements rather than replaces the InfoNCE anti-collapse objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: both sensors align the same bridge, yet one ranks river scenes nearest and the other city scenes. Consensus targets that geometric mismatch.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14496">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../multimodal-models/2611.14496-rs-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eb1672b725d557bc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="multimodal-models:rs-jepa" data-paper-title="RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="multimodal-models" data-theme="multimodal-models" data-topic="multimodal-models/world-state-actions">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Multimodal models / Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ef96d26f392f61c2">Why check stop-gradient and actual CUDA separately after matching the RS-JEPA loss value?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=multimodal-models%3Ars-jepa">RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-11-11 · Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Forgetting to detach the consensus target leaves the forward value unchanged but changes gradients. A cuda label also proves no device execution. An independent loop checks value and gradients; the CUDA diagnostic checks real tensor devices and backward work, not full Vim training or image retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Teaching example: a two-sample batch has one non-twin neighbour per row, so all distributions are one and KL is zero. Larger batches test gradients and sensor-swap invariance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 数据协议与代码映射, 结果、负控与边界, 高成本完整实验. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14496">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../multimodal-models/2611.14496-rs-jepa/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ef96d26f392f61c2">Question link</a></p>
</details>

<details class="ar-learning-guide" markdown="1"><summary>Topic guide and reading order</summary>

## Start with this question

Does the model only recognize a scene, or can it predict how an action changes the state?

## Takeaway

Learning prediction or control representations requires observations, actions, and future states together. LeWAM jointly learns latent future prediction and action flow matching so representation and policy shape each other. Planning uses latent dynamics to evaluate actions. WOVEN organizes generated video transitions as supervision controlled by scene, action, and reasoning type for consequences, causes, and counterfactuals. SWIM asks which state coordinates should contribute to latent distance. Offline inverse dynamics gates only future displacement; once frozen, sqrt(g) calibrates distances between same-frame pairs. Planning does not read future states.

## Example

Pushing a cup left and right on the same table should lead to different outcomes. Recognizing a cup does not control a robot. Latent prediction can avoid pixel reconstruction, but test whether actions matter, whether multistep rollouts drift, and whether selected actions reach goals in closed loop.

## Common pitfall

Realistic videos, low one-step error, or high training-set QA scores do not prove effective planning. Separate source scenes and trajectories by group and prevent counterfactuals from leaking future results. Local LeWAM is a non-held-out closed-loop diagnostic; WOVEN is a small experiment on public training data. Neither establishes the paper's full generalization or robotics claims.

## Reading order

Start with LeWAM's joint latent and action objective to see how prediction feeds control. Then read WOVEN on visual transitions and controlled supervision. Distinguish representation learning, synthetic data, question answering, and closed-loop planning. Follow up with visual geometry, video memory, or embodied actions.

1. [LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs](../../../../reproductions/2610.12818-lewam/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12818)
2. [WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs](../../../../reproductions/2610.12417-woven/README-en.md) · [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12417)

## Check your understanding

Does lower one-step latent MSE necessarily improve long-horizon control success?

??? note "Show suggested answer"

    No. Errors can fall in directions irrelevant to action choice, compound over a rollout, or be exploited by policy search. Compare closed-loop control with matched environments, goals, and budgets, and do not present training trajectories as held out.

</details>
